SQ2.brief: When you create a project, Unreal asks you to pick a template. A template is a starting point that decides what the project already contains. Third Person gives you a character you can control and a small level, while Blank gives you almost nothing. In this quest you create the project you will use for the rest of the Starter Quests, and you compare it with a Blank project to see the difference.
checklist: Create a new project named UC_Sandbox from the Third Person template. Choose Blueprint as the project type and keep Starter Content turned on.
Press Play and run around the level once.
Create and open a second project from the Blank template and compare the two. Notice that Blank has no pawn (no character to control) and no level art.
Close the Blank project. You will use UC_Sandbox for all the quests from here on.
SQ2.done_when: Send a screenshot of UC_Sandbox open in the editor, and add one sentence about what the Third Person template gives you that Blank does not.

SQ3.brief: The viewport is the large window in the middle of the editor that shows your level. You will move through it all day, so it is worth learning the controls well now. In this quest you fly the camera, save a camera position, and learn how to leave your character while the game is running so that you can look around.
checklist: Hold the right mouse button and use the W, A, S, D keys to fly, with Q and E to go down and up. While you fly, turn the mouse wheel to change the fly speed.
Select something in the level and press F. The camera moves to focus on it.
Save a camera bookmark, which is a stored camera position, with Ctrl+1. Move away, then press 1 to return to it.
Press Play to start Play in Editor (PIE). Then press F8 to eject, which lets you leave the character and fly around while the game keeps running.
Press Esc to stop PIE.
SQ3.done_when: Send a short text that says which key ejects you from PIE, and why you would want to do that.

SQ4.brief: Every file in an Unreal project is called an asset, and a project soon has hundreds of them. Clear folders and a short prefix on each name, such as SM_ for a Static Mesh, make it easy for anyone to find things later, including you. In this quest you make the folder structure used in Unrealcraft and give one asset of each kind its correct prefix.
checklist: Open the Content Drawer with Ctrl+Space. This is the panel that shows all the files of your project.
Create a folder at /Content/UC/ and add these subfolders inside it: Maps, Meshes, Materials, Textures, and Blueprints.

Rename or duplicate one asset of each kind so that it has the correct prefix: SM_ for a Static Mesh, M_ for a material, MI_ for a Material Instance, T_ for a texture, BP_ for a Blueprint, and L_ for a level.
Save a level with the name L_Sandbox in the folder UC/Maps.
SQ4.done_when: Send a screenshot of the UC folder tree that shows the assets with their prefixes.

SQ5.brief: Every object you place in a level is called an actor. Building anything in Unreal means moving, rotating and scaling actors, and doing it exactly is better than doing it by eye. In this quest you practice the transform tools, turn on snapping so that things move in fixed steps, and learn a few panels that help you place and organize actors.
checklist: Select an actor and press W to move it, E to rotate it and R to scale it. Pressing Space switches between these three tools.
Turn on grid snapping at the top of the viewport and set it to 10 or 50. Set the rotation snap to 15°.
In the Outliner, the panel that lists everything in the level, create a folder called Blockout and put 3 actors into it.
Select an actor and type an exact Location into its Details panel.
Open World Settings and find the setting named GameMode Override. You only need to find it for now.
Lift an actor so that it floats above the floor, then press End to drop it down onto the floor.
SQ5.done_when: Send a screenshot that shows the Outliner folder and a Details panel with the values you typed in.

SQ6.brief: A graybox is a level built from simple shapes with no art, so that you can test its size and layout early. In Unreal, one unit is one centimeter, and spaces must be sized to fit the character, not guessed. In this quest you build one small room with a doorway and a window, and then walk through it to feel whether the size is right.
checklist: Create a new level named L_Room_01. Build a floor, 4 walls, 1 doorway and 1 window, using cubes or the tools in Modeling Mode.
Size the doorway to fit the mannequin instead of guessing. For the default character, about 120 to 150 cm wide and 220 cm or more tall works well.
Place a Player Start actor, which is the point where the player appears. Rotate it so that its blue arrow points into the room.
Play in the editor (PIE) and walk through the door. Check that the ceiling does not feel too low above the character.
Take a screenshot from the eye level of the character.
SQ6.done_when: Send an eye-level screenshot of L_Room_01 in which the Player Start is visible, either in the Outliner or in the viewport.

SQ7.brief: Work that is too dark or flat is hard for anyone to review, so everyone should be able to do a basic lighting pass. The goal is not beauty yet: the goal is that a player can see the space and where to go. In this quest you add a sun, sky light and fog to your room with one tool, and then add one more light to make the doorway stand out.
checklist: Open L_Room_01. Open the Window menu and choose Env. Light Mixer. Use it to add a Directional Light (the sun), a Sky Light, a Sky Atmosphere and Height Fog.
Rotate the Directional Light until the sunlight comes in through the window.
Add one Point Light or Rect Light near the doorway so that the doorway stands out.
Check your result against the goal: the player can see where to go. It does not need to look pretty.
SQ7.done_when: Send one screenshot from before and one from after your lighting pass, both taken from the same camera bookmark.

SQ8.brief: A material decides how a surface looks, for example its color and how shiny it is. A Material Instance is a light copy of a material in which you can only change the values the original left open, which are called parameters. It is the normal way to recolor things in Unreal because the change shows at once. In this quest you make one instance, change one value in it, and put it on a wall.
checklist: Find a material that has parameters. You can use one from the Starter Content or one that came with the template.
Right-click the material, choose Create Material Instance, and name the new asset MI_Wall_Accent.
Open the instance and change one parameter in it, such as a color or the roughness.
Apply the instance to one wall in L_Room_01, for example by dragging it onto the wall.
SQ8.done_when: Send a screenshot that shows the instance editor with the changed parameter, next to the wall that uses it.

SQ9.brief: A Blueprint is Unreal's visual way to add behavior: you connect boxes called nodes instead of writing code. An overlap is the moment when one object starts touching another, and it is the most common way to make the world react to the player. In this quest you build one small interactive object, either a pickup or a door, that reacts when the player touches it.
checklist: Choose ONE of these two: a pickup that prints a message and disappears, or a door that opens when the player overlaps it.
Create a Blueprint of type Actor and name it BP_Pickup or BP_Door. Add a mesh to it, and add a Box Collision or Sphere Collision that will detect the player.
In the graph, add the event On Component Begin Overlap for the collision and connect it to a Print String node. After that, add Destroy Actor for the pickup, or move the door.
Place your Blueprint in L_Room_01 and trigger it while you play in the editor (PIE).
SQ9.done_when: Send a short clip recorded in PIE, or 2 screenshots (one before and one after the interaction). Also send a screenshot of the Blueprint graph.

SQ10.brief: A room can look right from the editor camera and still feel wrong when you walk through it as the player. The GameMode is the asset that holds the rules of the game, including which character the player controls, and each level can choose its own. In this quest you make sure your room uses the Third Person character, walk through it, and fix one thing that feels wrong.
checklist: Open L_Room_01 and open World Settings. Set GameMode Override to the Third Person GameMode.
Play in the editor (PIE). Walk, jump, and bump into every wall.
Drag a mannequin mesh from the Content Browser into the room. Leave it standing there as a fixed reference for size.
Note one thing that feels wrong, such as a tight corner or a ledge that is too high, and fix it.
SQ10.done_when: Send a short text that says what you fixed, and a screenshot of the mannequin standing in the space.

SQ11.brief: Unreal gives you two ways to build game logic: Blueprint, where you connect nodes, and C++, a programming language you type. Each one is better for some jobs, and most games use both. In this quest you only read about the difference, so that you know what C++ is for even if you never write it.
checklist: Read the Blueprint vs C++ page. You do not need an IDE, which is a program for writing code.
Write 3 lines: one thing that is better done in Blueprint, one thing that is better done in C++, and one thing you are not sure about.

SQ13.brief: Mentors can only review what they can read. A screenshot of a Blueprint graph or a Details panel is not useful if the text is too small to read, and many people look at it on a phone. In this quest you try Unreal's High Resolution Screenshot tool and take one editor screenshot that stays readable on a small screen.
checklist: Use the High Resolution Screenshot tool once. It takes a picture of the viewport at a higher resolution than your screen.
Take one screenshot of the editor in which a graph or the Details panel can still be read at the size of a phone screen, and attach it.
SQ13.done_when: Send one screenshot of a graph that is easy to read.

SQ14.brief: Some things cannot be shown in a still picture, such as a door that opens or a character that moves. For these you send a short video clip of the game running in the editor, which is called Play in Editor or PIE. In this quest you record a short clip, cut it down to the important part, and attach it.
checklist: Record 10 to 20 seconds of PIE with a screen recorder such as OBS, Game Bar, or a similar program. Then trim the clip so that only the useful part is left.
Attach the clip as a video file.
SQ14.done_when: Send your clip as a video file. It must be shorter than 20 seconds.

SQ15.brief: When you are stuck, a clear question gets a fast answer and an unclear one often gets no answer. The #help-desk channel on the Discord server has a template for help posts and a pinned example of a bad post. In this quest you rewrite that bad example so that it follows the template.
checklist: Find the pinned bad example in #help-desk and rewrite it so that it follows the template. Paste your rewritten post as your proof.
SQ15.done_when: Send your rewritten post as text.

SQ16.brief: Giving useful feedback is a skill, and practicing it also teaches you to look at your own work more clearly. Good feedback is specific: it says what works, what the problem is, and what to do next. In this quest you write that kind of feedback on a post by another member in the #showcase channel.
checklist: Pick a post by someone else in #showcase and write a comment on it that names 1 thing that works, 1 specific issue, and 1 next step. Then paste the link to your comment.
SQ16.done_when: Send the link to your review comment.

SQ17.brief: Showing unfinished work and hearing what is wrong with it is how you get better quickly. It is easier when you ask one specific question, because then people know what kind of feedback you want. In this quest you post a work in progress (WIP), and then answer the feedback you receive.
checklist: Post a work in progress (WIP) in #showcase and ask one specific question about it.
Reply to the feedback you get, and say what you will change, or why you will not change it. Then paste the link to that reply.
SQ17.done_when: Send the link to the thread.

SQ12.brief: Keyboard shortcuts let you do common actions without looking for a button, and a few of them save a lot of time every week. In this quest you learn five shortcuts for the level editor and decide which one will help you the most.
checklist: Try each of these shortcuts in the editor: G switches game view on and off, Ctrl+B finds the selected asset in the Content Browser, Alt+drag makes a copy of an actor, H hides the selected actor and Ctrl+H shows hidden actors again, and F11 makes the viewport fullscreen.
Write which one of them you will use the most, and when you will use it.
SQ12.done_when: Send a short text that says which shortcut you will use most and when.
